role: author-derived, frozen before options; not an independent review

solutions.written_task: 1. How can coherent light waves be obtained?
solutions.task: Explain how to obtain coherent light waves and identify the frequency and phase relationship preserved by the method.
solutions.source_solution: Split one beam into two parts, send them along different paths, and bring them together again. With stable relative optical paths and a path difference compatible with the beam's coherence, the parts retain the same frequency and a stable phase difference, supporting stable interference. Coherence does not require zero phase difference; two independent ordinary sources of the same colour or frequency do not by themselves guarantee a stable phase difference.
conditions: Split and recombine one beam.
Stable relative optical paths and a path difference compatible with the beam's coherence.
Same frequency and stable phase difference, not necessarily zero phase difference.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Distinguish a stable phase relationship inherited from a common beam from merely matching colour, matching frequency, or switching lamps on together.
solutions.production_loss: Recognizing a complete arrangement does not demonstrate unaided written recall or designing and building that arrangement.

solutions.written_task: 2. What is the phenomenon of light interference?
solutions.task: Explain strengthening and weakening through wave superposition, distinguishing local darkness from the disappearance of energy.
solutions.source_solution: Where light waves meet, their vibrations superpose. Their phase relationship strengthens the resultant vibration at some positions and weakens it at others; coherent light can produce a stable bright-and-dark distribution. Vibrations add, so intensity is not simply the sum of the separate intensities everywhere. In the ideal case, opposite vibrations with equal amplitudes can cancel completely, whereas unequal amplitudes leave a remainder. Dark regions receive less energy, but interference neither destroys energy nor necessarily converts it to heat; it redistributes energy flow.
conditions: A stable pattern requires coherent superposition.
Complete cancellation additionally requires the appropriate phase relationship and equal amplitudes.
Keep conservation in the non-absorbing ideal model separate from real absorption.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Distinguish a spatial bright-and-dark pattern caused by superposed vibrations from adding intensities everywhere or destroying energy in destructive interference.
solutions.production_loss: Recognizing a complete explanation does not demonstrate composing an unaided written definition.

solutions.written_task: 3. Which physical property of light waves is associated with differences in colour?
solutions.task: Relate the colour of single-frequency light to frequency and handle the limitation of comparing wavelengths across media.
solutions.source_solution: For the single-frequency visible light considered here, colour differences are associated with frequency; vacuum wavelength can also label that frequency. Crossing a stationary interface preserves frequency while speed and in-medium wavelength may change, so wavelengths measured in different media cannot be interpreted directly as a change of colour. Amplitude mainly concerns brightness and relative phase concerns interference; neither replaces the frequency distinction. This does not claim that the perceived colour of mixed light is determined by one frequency.
conditions: Single-frequency visible light, not a one-frequency description of every mixed colour.
A stationary interface.
Separate vacuum wavelength labels from in-medium wavelengths.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Unchanged frequency is compatible with changed in-medium wavelength; colour is not an amplitude, phase, or arbitrary in-medium-wavelength label.
solutions.production_loss: Recognizing the frequency explanation does not demonstrate unaided written recall of the relationship and its medium qualification.

solutions.written_task: 4. After a transparent block of ice is struck with a stone, the cracks show rainbow-coloured glints. Why does this happen?
solutions.task: Under explicit conditions, explain coloured ice-fracture glints by interference of reflections from the two sides of a thin air layer, without asking the learner to make fractures.
solutions.source_solution: Model an already observed fracture as a very thin air gap, with suitable white-light illumination and reflections from its two sides able to overlap. The two reflected waves come from the same incident light but follow different paths; their relative phase depends on gap thickness, viewing angle, wavelength, and reflection phase changes. Different frequencies in white light are strengthened or weakened by different amounts, changing the colour proportions of the remaining reflection and allowing coloured glints. The fracture is not a light source and need not convert light into new frequencies. Not every fracture has the necessary gap and overlap conditions, so the effect is not guaranteed. The ice-air-ice interface sequence differs from air-coating-glass, so the green antireflection coating's quarter-wavelength rule cannot simply be reused; the source also supplies no data for a unique numerical gap thickness.
conditions: A very thin air gap.
Suitable white-light illumination.
Reflections from both sides can overlap and produce observable interference.
A conditional explanation, not a claim about every fracture or a determined thickness.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Distinguish frequency-selective strengthening and weakening from emission by a fracture, frequency conversion, or inevitable rainbow glints in every fracture.
solutions.production_loss: Recognizing the complete mechanism does not demonstrate building the thin-layer model or writing its conditional explanation unaided; no gap thickness is measured and no fracture is made.

solutions.written_task: 5. In water, the wavelength decreases to $\frac{1}{n}$ of its value in air ($n$ is the refractive index of water relative to air). Does this mean that a diver underwater cannot see surrounding objects in natural light?
solutions.task: Use the refractive index of water relative to air to relate wavelength, speed, and frequency, and decide whether the shorter wavelength makes natural light invisible.
solutions.source_solution: No. For each frequency component, the stationary air-water interface preserves frequency, and the relative refractive index gives $v_{\mathrm{water}}=v_{\mathrm{air}}/n$. From $v=f\lambda$, $\lambda_{\mathrm{water}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{air}}/n$ while $f_{\mathrm{water}}=f_{\mathrm{air}}$. The shorter in-medium wavelength does not shift a visible frequency outside the visible range. A diver can still see objects when enough visible light reaches the eyes from them. This does not guarantee clear vision at every depth or turbidity, or perfectly unchanged object colours: propagation losses can change the proportions of frequencies reaching the eyes.
conditions: $n$ is the index of water relative to air; no numerical value is invented.
A stationary interface preserves frequency.
Enough visible light reaches the eyes from the object; distinguish wavelength change from propagation losses.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Distinguish a shorter wavelength from a higher frequency, avoiding direct application of a vacuum visible-wavelength range to wavelengths in water.
solutions.production_loss: Recognizing the full argument does not demonstrate unaided use of $v=f\lambda$ or composing the explanation of underwater visibility.

solutions.written_task: 6. List the main applications of interference.
solutions.task: Collectively identify the source-listed main applications, rather than recognizing antireflection alone.
solutions.source_solution: Main applications include interferometers using fringe and optical-path changes for precise measurement of light wavelength, measurement of gas refractive index, and specialized tests; the source specifically lists surface-quality inspection through fringe changes. Another category is antireflection treatment of camera lenses, projector lenses, periscopes, and similar instruments: film thickness sets the reflected waves' relative phase and refractive index helps match amplitudes, reducing reflection and stray light to improve transmitted imaging. In the transparent, non-absorbing ideal model, reduced reflected energy becomes transmitted energy rather than amplified or newly created light; real losses prevent a guarantee of complete transmission. A green-light antireflection coating is not a filter transmitting only violet light.
conditions: Collectively cover the four source-listed applications: wavelength measurement, gas-index measurement, surface-quality inspection, and antireflection treatment.
Surface inspection is an application fact listed in allowed lesson prose 2 and 3, not an additional selected concept or a reference to an unselected figure.
Do not add unlisted medical, communications, or other applications.
Retain antireflection phase, amplitude, and non-absorption qualifications; it is not optical amplification.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Judge applications and mechanisms as one complete collection, distinguishing interference measurement and antireflection from frequency recolouring or energy amplification.
solutions.production_loss: Selecting supplied applications does not demonstrate unaided recall and listing of all main applications; content coverage of four applications is not evidence of free-list production.
